extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants, biomedical researchers, postdocs, and academic PIs
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, experience-based guidance and commentary about NIH grant review, resubmission rules, critique interpretation, and related career issues for biomedical researchers preparing or responding to NIH reviews. Mixes reviewer-template changes with career/grantsmanship advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not contact study section chair or members
rubrics_metrics.description: You are absolutely forbidden from contacting the study section chair (or any other member of the study section) regarding your application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contacting study section members about your application is prohibited and pointless; do not attempt to reach or lobby individual reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: SRO contact limited to pre-review issues
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not impermissible to contact the SRO of the study section, but it is pointless, as they are only supposed to engage with you on issues relating to your application that arise prior to review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve SRO contact for administrative or pre-review problems only; do not expect substantive review interpretation from the SRO after review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program Officer is point person after review
rubrics_metrics.description: Once your application has been reviewed, your PO becomes the point person for discussing the outcome of review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-review discussions should go through your PO; be aware that the PO's information is generally limited to the written critiques and their own experience with the study section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experienced PIs and former/current reviewers to interpret critiques
rubrics_metrics.description: Your best resource for helping you interpret your written critiques is other PIs who have had grants reviewed, discussed, and scored by that study section, as well as any colleagues who are former/current members of the study section, but who did not serve the cycle in which your grant was reviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These individuals can explain study-section biases, preferences, and help you 'read between the lines' of critiques; if unavailable, seek colleagues with broad review experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not appeal review outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t even think about appealing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals are discouraged/pointless as a route to change review outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written critiques may not state the real fatal problems
rubrics_metrics.description: What the critiques *say* were the key problems with your application aren’t necessarily what really sank it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret critiques critically and use experienced readers to identify underlying reasons beyond the literal text.

rubrics_metrics.name: RPG Overall Impact now requires a paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: The Overall Impact section now has eliminated the bulleted list and requires a paragraph: 'Write a paragraph summarizing the factors that informed your Overall Impact score.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers must provide a narrative summary explaining factors behind the Overall Impact score, rather than only bulleted strengths/weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH five review criteria retained (Strengths/Weaknesses format)
rubrics_metrics.description: The subsections for the five review criteria (Significance, Innovation, Approach, Investigator, and Environment) still incorporate the bulleted list Strengths and Weaknesses format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each criterion subsection should list bulleted strengths and weaknesses even though Overall Impact moved to a paragraph format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance (NIH review criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Significance — one of the five NIH review criteria used to evaluate Research Project Grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsection uses bulleted Strengths and Weaknesses; assess the importance of the problem or critical barrier addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation (NIH review criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovation — one of the five NIH review criteria used to evaluate Research Project Grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsection uses bulleted Strengths and Weaknesses; assess novelty of concepts, approaches, or technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach (NIH review criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach — one of the five NIH review criteria used to evaluate Research Project Grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsection uses bulleted Strengths and Weaknesses; assess rigor, feasibility, and appropriateness of methods and analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigator (NIH review criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigator — one of the five NIH review criteria used to evaluate Research Project Grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsection uses bulleted Strengths and Weaknesses; assess qualifications, experience, and productivity of key personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environment (NIH review criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Environment — one of the five NIH review criteria used to evaluate Research Project Grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsection uses bulleted Strengths and Weaknesses; assess institutional support, resources, and collaborative climate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall Impact score and percentile definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall Impact Score is the average final score from 1-9 given to the grant application by all the members of the study section, x10, and rounded (up?) to the nearest whole number. The percentile is the percent of applications reviewed by that same study section over the current round and the previous two that had better impact scores than that, and rounded up to the nearest whole number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand how numeric scores are averaged and converted to percentiles when interpreting review outcomes and funding likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study-section-specific scoring behavior (score inflation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different study sections show dramatic differences in scoring behavior (e.g., percent of grants scored better than 20 or 30 varies widely between sections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not interpret raw percentiles or scores without considering the scoring norms and 'inflation' tendencies of the specific study section that reviewed your application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institute/Council funding policies can override percentile (e.g., NIGMS guidelines for well-funded labs)
rubrics_metrics.description: A small number of applications with percentile scores better than the 20th percentile for which awards have not been made. Most of these correspond to new (Type 1, not competing renewal) applications that are subject to the NIGMS Council’s funding decision guidelines for well-funded laboratories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that programmatic or council-level policies (such as de-prioritizing new awards to already well-funded labs) can lead to non-funding despite good percentiles; know institute-specific policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about repurposing unfunded A1 into new A0 (resubmission rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any of you who have repurposed an unfunded A1 into a new A0 — the author is asking whether such grants were accepted as new or rejected as an impermissible resubmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repurposing a previously reviewed/resubmitted application into a supposedly 'new' application risks being judged an impermissible resubmission; be careful and document changes if pursuing this route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not contact or attempt to phone individual reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't bother trying to get that motherfucker Scarpa on the motherfucken phone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directly contacting reviewers (by phone or otherwise) is inappropriate and futile; use official channels (PO) instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure proper controls and avoid cherry-picking
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to perform appropriate controls (e.g., to distinguish complementation from spontaneous reversion) or cherry-picking data can lead to irreproducible results and retractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and report rigorous controls and reproducible assays; confirm findings by reliable methods before publication or claiming results in grant applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship should reflect true contributions; avoid excessive equal-contributor claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of papers listing multiple authors as 'contributed equally' (e.g., four equal co-first/last authors) — this strains credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use authorship designations responsibly and accurately; ensure contribution statements meaningfully reflect who did what.

rubrics_metrics.name: New PIs must work effectively with less-experienced postdocs to produce publications
rubrics_metrics.description: When you first start your own lab... you have no choice but to get yourself off the ground with less talented post-docs... one of your most difficult and important tasks as a new PI is to enable these people—despite their limitations—to fulfill all of their potential and succeed at publishing good papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in mentoring and developing early trainees; publications and awarded grants are necessary to later attract higher-tier talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postdoctoral training functions as selection; longer postdocs can be appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-doctoral training is also about selection: identifying the most talented and accomplished scientists to give a shot at scientific independence. Longer post-docs should be welcomed as they provide a much fairer opportunity to prove one’s mettle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a uniform two-year postdoc is sufficient; evaluate progression over time—lack of productivity after 5+ years may indicate unsuitability for an independent PI role.
